Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette:
Arthur, a 66-year-old software engineer, presented with a quiet demeanor, his life now overshadowed by a pervasive sense of unease that had intensified over the past few years. He spoke sparingly about his childhood, only hinting at years of unpredictable physical abuse at the hands of a caregiver. He recalled the biting cold of the unheated room where he was sometimes confined and the rough, sudden grasp that would leave his young heart pounding in his chest. Those early experiences, long buried, had laid a foundation for his current struggles.

Now, even decades later, certain sensations instantly transported him back to that terrifying helplessness. A specific temperature on his skin, perhaps a cool draft in his office, could suddenly evoke a vivid, intrusive memory of the abuse, bringing with it a wave of anxiety. When these memories surged, Arthur found himself consumed by the conviction that people simply couldn't be trusted, a deep-seated belief that had been forged in his early experiences. This persistent mistrust, a core negative appraisal, made him increasingly wary of others, leading him to actively avoid social contacts, even with colleagues he once enjoyed. He had come to believe he was permanently an outsider, a belief reinforced each time he chose isolation.

His internal state further perpetuated this cycle. His own heart racing or pounding, a physiological echo of past terror, frequently acted as a potent trigger. When his body responded this way, Arthur would instantly feel a heightened sense of threat; he was certain that his body reacted to danger before his mind even had time to process it, a terrifying lack of control. This perceived bodily betrayal fueled his negative appraisals, cementing his belief that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next, leading to constant vigilance. This hyper-vigilance, in turn, primed him to notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, whether it was a sharp letter opener on a colleague's desk or a heavy stapler, further elevating his sense of impending threat. Living under this constant, elevated sense of threat, Arthur found that almost any unexpected sound or movement could suddenly morph into a new, potent trigger for his anxiety.

The insidious nature of his negative appraisals meant that his general mistrust and constant vigilance became self-fulfilling. His mind, perpetually on alert for danger, now seemed to interpret even benign tactile sensations or internal physical cues as threats, effectively broadening the range of things that could trigger his anxiety. Consequently, his fear of the unknown and his certainty that danger lurked around every corner meant he was constantly on edge, making him jump and react with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly, even his wife. To manage this overwhelming apprehension, Arthur developed a range of maladaptive strategies. He began to avoid paying attention to or even looking at his own body, particularly when he felt his heart rate increase, hoping to escape the distressing sensations. He also rigorously avoided any form of physical contact with others, creating an emotional and physical distance that left him feeling increasingly isolated.

These avoidance strategies, however, only tightened the loop. By avoiding social contacts, he inadvertently confirmed his belief that he was an outsider and that people couldn't be trusted, deepening his negative appraisals. In his work as a software engineer, this meant he rarely participated in team meetings and stopped going to lunch with his co-workers, leading to a noticeable decline in his collaborative output and a sense of growing alienation from his team. His avoidance of his own body also meant he never learned that his racing heart was often a harmless anxiety response, thus maintaining it as a powerful trigger. Furthermore, his efforts to avoid being touched, while offering temporary relief, only served to heighten his startle response, making him even more sensitive and reactive to accidental physical contact, thus exacerbating his perception of threat. This spiraling pattern of avoidance, hyper-vigilance, and mistrust had left Arthur feeling profoundly alone and perpetually unsafe, prompting him to finally seek help, exhausted by the relentless grip of a past he could not outrun.
